newsitem.title: INDIA: India rupee convertibility route seen as ambitious.
newsitem.headline: India rupee convertibility route seen as ambitious.

text.p: Making the Indian rupee fully convertible by the end of the century is a tall order, bankers and economists said on Tuesday after the release of an official report mapping out a route to freeing the exchange rate.
A committee appointed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) submitted its recommendations, listing preconditions needed before the rupee can be made convertible on the current account.

The conditions include an average inflation rate of three to five percent for the three-year period until 2000, and a reduction in the fiscal deficit to 3.5 percent of GDP by the financial year 1999/2000.
"These are very difficult numbers to achieve going by our past record," Subir Biswas, senior treasurer at ABN-AMRO Bank, said.
"It might take more time than three years."
While there were reservations about the speed at which the rupee's value can be put in the lap of the markets, there was praise for the committee's approach.
"In terms of direction, it (the recommendations) are good," R. Balakrishnan, president of Dil Vikas Finance, said. "But whether we can achieve the conditions is a matter of concern."
Analysts pointed out that the Indian inflation rate had averaged six to seven percent and seldom fallen below five percent.
The fiscal deficit as a percentage of GDP has been more than five percent, although the government has targeted reducing it to 4.5 percent in 1997/98 financial year (April-March).
The panel also said a total deregulation of interest rates should precede full convertibility on the capital account, adding that it should take place this year and next.

A decision on the recommendations will have to be taken by the finance ministry and some of the changes, such as amending of the RBI Act giving the central bank more independence, will require parliament's approval, analysts said.
The committee argued the Act should be amended to allow the central bank a freer hand in pursuing inflation targets.
"Its recommendations like allowing Indian residents to invest in overseas markets may face political barriers, delaying the whole process," Anindya Chatterjee, economist at NatWest Markets said.
Left-wing parties, especially communists, in the ruling United Front have been opposing the coalition's free-market policies.
A forex dealer at a European bank in Bombay said the Indian economy was not structurally prepared for full convertibility.
"I don't see full convertibility in three to five years," he said.
He said the absence of a deep and liquid money market and absence of term money market were a hindrance.
"Even our reserves are not enough for full convertibility," he said. India's forex reserves are close to $28 billion, compared to annual Indian imports of about $35 billion.
"The market was not expecting any bold or immediate steps," said an official of an American bank in Bombay.
He said the recent battering of some of the Southeast Asian currencies, such as the Thai baht, may have led the Indian panel to take a cautious approach.
The committee's report stressed the need for a constant review of progress towards the various pre-conditions and the said flexibility in policy was required.
Analysts said full convertibility in the current scenario would only aggravate the central bank's dilemma in trying to arrest the rupee's rise.
The RBI has been buying dollars to prevent the rupee rising but the consequent injection of excess liquidity into the domestic money supply has worried the central bank, analysts said.
The rupee was quoted around 35.78 to the dollar on Tuesday.
"There is no great urgency for full convertibility," said another banker.
